items.title: Keep Pace With Jehovah’s Celestial Chariot
items.answer:
This part begins with the video “Introduction to Ezekiel.” Play it, then draw out the two points with the audience and conclude with the meditation question.

1. The heavenly part of Jehovah’s organization is represented by an immense celestial chariot that is supremely fast and maneuverable. “The wheels and their structure appeared to glow like chrysʹo·lite, and the four of them looked alike. Their appearance and structure looked as though a wheel were within a wheel. When they moved, they could go in any of the four directions without turning as they went. Their rims were so high that they inspired awe, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.” (Eze 1:16-18) A chariot like that never has to turn around — whatever direction Jehovah’s organization must move in, it moves instantly and perfectly.

2. Jehovah himself controls the chariot’s movement: “They would go where the spirit inclined them to go, wherever the spirit went.” (Eze 1:20) And above the chariot Ezekiel saw the throne of Jehovah, whose appearance was “like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day… the appearance of the glory of Jehovah.” (Eze 1:26-28) The organization is not steering itself — God is in the chariot.

FOR MEDITATION — What must I do to keep pace with the celestial chariot? Stay close: keep feeding on Jehovah’s Word, attend the meetings, accept new direction from his organization promptly, and never let love of former ways or of personal comfort slow my step. The chariot moves at Jehovah’s speed, not mine — so I adjust my pace to his.

scriptures.quote: The wheels and their structure appeared to glow like chrysʹo·lite, and the four of them looked alike. Their appearance and structure looked as though a wheel were within a wheel. When they moved, they could go in any of the four directions without turning as they went. Their rims were so high that they inspired awe, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.

They would go where the spirit inclined them to go, wherever the spirit went. The wheels would be lifted up together with them, for the spirit operating on the living creatures was also in the wheels.

Above the expanse that was over their heads was what looked like a sapphire stone, and it resembled a throne. Sitting on the throne up above was someone whose appearance resembled that of a human. I saw something glowing like electrum that was like a fire radiating from what appeared to be his waist and upward; and from his waist down, I saw something that resembled fire. There was a brilliance all around him ... like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day. That was how the surrounding brilliant light appeared. It was like the appearance of the glory of Jehovah. When I saw it, I fell facedown and began to hear the voice of someone speaking.

items.cite: video “Introduction to Ezekiel”; rr 37-38 pars. 18-19; rr 38-39 pars. 21-24

items.title: Spiritual Gems
items.answer:
Answer to the assigned gem — Eze 1:6, 10: What do the four faces of each cherub in Ezekiel’s vision illustrate?
The four faces picture four outstanding qualities of Jehovah, perfectly balanced in him: the face of a man pictures love, the lion’s face justice, the bull’s face power, and the eagle’s face wisdom. No single face dominated the others — each cherub had all four at once. Jehovah never leans too far toward one quality; his justice is always tempered with love, and his power always moves with wisdom.

What I learned from this week’s Bible reading (Ezekiel 1-2):

1. Nothing escapes the notice of Jehovah’s organization. “Their rims were so high that they inspired awe, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.” (Eze 1:18) Jehovah sees everything happening to his people — nothing done against us is hidden from him, and nothing we do for him goes unnoticed either.

2. Faithfulness does not depend on how others respond. Jehovah told Ezekiel: “You must speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are a rebellious people.” (Eze 2:7) In Jehovah’s service, success is measured by faithfulness, not by results.

3. Jehovah’s servants need Jehovah’s strengthening, and he gives it. “When he spoke to me, spirit came into me and made me stand up on my feet so that I could hear the One speaking to me.” (Eze 2:2) Ezekiel was overwhelmed — face to face with the glory of God and sent to a rebellious house — and Jehovah empowered him for the assignment he was given.

Practical examples from these scriptures — how they have helped, or can help:
• Eze 1:10 can help me imitate Jehovah’s balance: at home or at work, when I am tempted to use all my “power” or demand strict “justice,” I first mix in love and wisdom — correcting a child with love, or a workmate with wisdom instead of a blast of criticism.
• Eze 1:18 has helped me under discouragement: when someone wronged me and nobody else saw it, remembering that the rims are “full of eyes all around” kept bitterness from taking root — Jehovah saw it, and he will handle it.
• Eze 2:7 steadies me in the ministry: when people are cold or dismissive, I remember Ezekiel — my work is to speak Jehovah’s words kindly and faithfully; whether they listen is their choice before Jehovah.
• Eze 2:2 reminds me to pray for holy spirit before a hard conversation or assignment — the strength to stand up and do the work comes from Jehovah, not from feeling brave.

scriptures.quote: Their rims were so high that they inspired awe, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.
You must speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are a rebellious people.
When he spoke to me, spirit came into me and made me stand up on my feet so that I could hear the One speaking to me.

items.title: Bible Reading — Eze 2:1-10 (th study 2)
items.answer:
Context: Jehovah commissions Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel whether they listen or not, and shows him a scroll covered with dirges, mourning and wailing — the message he must deliver is heavy, and it must first become part of him.

Lesson 1: Jehovah’s servant must deliver God’s message faithfully regardless of the response (Eze 2:7). Lesson 2: Like Ezekiel, we must take in God’s Word fully before we speak it to others (Eze 2:8-10).

Possible comment: “You must speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are a rebellious people.” (Eze 2:7) Ezekiel’s success was not measured by how Israel responded but by how faithfully he spoke. That steadies me in the ministry today: when people are cold or dismissive, I have still done my work well if I delivered Jehovah’s message with kindness and respect.

scriptures.quote: You must speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are a rebellious people.

items.title: Starting a Conversation — House to House (lmd lesson 3 point 3)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 3 point 3 — “Empathize with the person. Try to imagine how he feels. Ask yourself: ‘What may he be concerned about? What might he find helpful and appealing?’ Doing so will help you to show kindness in a natural and sincere manner. Show that you care about what matters to a person by listening. If he tells you how he feels about something or mentions a problem he is facing, do not change the subject.”

HOUSE TO HOUSE — Daniel offers a Bible study, and the whole conversation is conducted around that point: he listens, shows he cares, and lets kindness — not a sales pitch — open the door.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good afternoon! I’m Daniel, one of your neighbours — from just round the corner. We’re out sharing something that has helped many families in this area."
Ruth (Householder): "Oh, hello. Sorry — I’m a bit distracted this morning."
Daniel (Publisher): "No problem at all. You seem to have a lot on your mind — is everything okay?"
Ruth (Householder): "It’s my mother. She’s not been well for almost a year now, and I’m the one looking after her. Some days I feel I just can’t carry on."
Daniel (Publisher): "I’m really sorry to hear that. Caring for a sick parent takes so much out of a person — the worry, the tiredness, watching someone you love suffer. That is a heavy load to carry."
Ruth (Householder): "It is. And people keep telling me to be strong, but nobody asks how I actually feel."
Daniel (Publisher): "How do you feel, Ruth? I mean it — I’d like to know."
Ruth (Householder): "Honestly? Guilty, sometimes. If I rest, I feel I’m failing her."
Daniel (Publisher): "Thank you for telling me. May I share something that has helped me? The Bible speaks directly to people in your situation — it says God cares for those who feel they can’t cope, and it holds out the hope of a time when sickness and death will be gone forever. Many people have found a free Bible study programme a real support while they carry a load like yours — short sessions, your own questions, at your pace. Would you like to see how it works?"
Ruth (Householder): "Honestly… that sounds like something I could use right now."
Daniel (Publisher): "Then let me show you a sample lesson — about ten minutes, and you can decide afterwards if you’d like to continue. We ‘rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep,’ and I’d be glad to walk through this with you."
Ruth (Householder): "Okay — come in for a few minutes."

Keys: Daniel conducted the whole offer around lmd lesson 3 point 3 — kindness shown through empathy. He imagined her situation before he spoke, listened when she mentioned her problem instead of changing the subject, and asked how she felt. Only then did he offer the Bible study — framed around what SHE finds helpful and appealing, so the kindness made the offer natural and sincere rather than pushy.

scriptures.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.

items.cite: lmd lesson 3 point 3; SEE ALSO Rom. 12:15, 16

items.title: Making Disciples — Family Opposition (lmd lesson 11 point 5)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 11 point 5 — “Use illustrations carefully. Before using an illustration, ask yourself: ‘Is the illustration simple?’ ‘Will my student easily understand it?’ ‘Will it help my student to remember the main point—not just the illustration?’”

MAKING DISCIPLES — Daniel encourages his Bible student Ruth, who is dealing with family opposition, using one simple illustration that carries the main point.

Daniel (Publisher): "Ruth, thank you for keeping our study time today — I know it isn’t easy."
Ruth (Householder): "Honestly, Daniel, I nearly cancelled. My husband says I’m wasting my time with this ‘religion of yours.’ Some days I feel like giving up."
Daniel (Publisher): "I’m sorry — that must hurt, especially coming from family. May I ask you something? When the wind blows against you, does the wind decide whether you reach home?"
Ruth (Householder): "What do you mean?"
Daniel (Publisher): "Think of riding a bicycle into a strong wind. The wind pushes hard, but the rider decides: keep pedalling, keep the direction. The wind can make the trip harder — it cannot change where you’re going."
Ruth (Householder): "So the opposition is the wind… and Jehovah is the one taking me home?"
Daniel (Publisher): "Exactly. Family opposition is painful, but it cannot stop you from reaching Jehovah — only your own decision can. Remember Joseph: his own brothers sold him, yet he kept serving God, and in the end he was able to save his whole family."
Ruth (Householder): "I hadn’t thought of it that way. The picture of the wind will stay with me."
Daniel (Publisher): "Good — that is the main point, and you said it in your own words. Next week we continue in our lesson. And your husband is welcome to sit in any time he likes — no pressure on him at all."
Ruth (Householder): "I’ll invite him. Thank you, Daniel."

Keys: Daniel applied lmd lesson 11 point 5 — he tested his illustration before using it: it was simple (a bicycle against the wind), Ruth understood it immediately, and it made her remember the main point — opposition cannot stop her course — not just the picture. He kept the encouragement brief and let the simple illustration do the work.

items.title: Talk — God’s Kingdom Will Replace Human Governments (lmd appendix A point 22; th study 6)
items.answer:
THEME: God’s Kingdom Will Replace Human Governments. (lmd appendix A point 22; th study 6)

Good morning, brothers and sisters. Every person alive today lives under some human government. Some are kind, some cruel, all imperfect. So a question that touches every one of us is: Will things always be this way? The Bible answers with a clear no — and it tells us exactly what will replace human rule.

Consider the world scene for a moment. Leaders promise peace and prosperity, yet wars continue, corruption is exposed year after year, and the gap between rich and poor widens. Why can no government fix these problems? Because of what Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar nearly 2,600 years ago: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.” (Daniel 2:44) Notice — the kingdom that replaces human governments will not be set up by politicians, by revolution, or by any assembly of nations. It is set up by the God of heaven himself. That is why it “will never be destroyed.”

Daniel saw that kingdom in a dream. Human governments were pictured by an immense image — a head of gold, chest of silver, abdomen of copper, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay: kingdoms that rise and fall, each more divided than the last. And what happened to that image? A stone was cut out, not by human hands. It struck the image on its feet, crushed them, and the stone became a mountain that filled the whole earth. The meaning is unmistakable: God’s Kingdom will strike the present system of things at a moment no human expects, and human governments will not survive the blow. Daniel said it plainly — that Kingdom will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms, and it alone will stand forever.

Why should that move us rather than frighten us? Because of what that Kingdom is. Its King is Jesus Christ, God’s appointed Son, who has already proved his love by laying down his life for us. His government will not be a committee of quarrelling parties; it will be one righteous administration reaching to the ends of the earth. Under it, the things every honest heart longs for — peace, justice, good health, secure homes, enough food — will not be election promises. They will be law.

Compare the two, then. Human governments promise what they cannot deliver; God’s Kingdom delivers what no human can promise. Human governments pass away with every crisis; God’s Kingdom will never be destroyed and never be passed on to any other people.

So what should we do with this conviction? First, keep telling people — many of our neighbours are desperate for good news, and this is the best news there is. Second, keep living as citizens of that Kingdom now: its laws, its values, its unity. And third, keep praying for God’s Kingdom to come, as Jesus taught. When we pray that way, we are asking God to do what no human can — to replace every human government with the only government that will never fail.

Human governments have had their day. God’s day is coming — the stone cut out without hands is already on its way. May we be found standing on the side of that Kingdom when it strikes.

scriptures.quote: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed. And this kingdom will not be passed on to any other people. It will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms, and it alone will stand forever,

items.cite: lmd appendix A point 22 · th study 6 · Daniel 2:44

items.title: Congregation Bible Study — Walk Courageously With God, chap. 19
items.answer: Study source: the book Walk Courageously With God! (wcg), chapter 19, “They Fulfilled a Difficult Vow” — the account of Jephthah and his daughter (wcg chap. 19 pp. 90-93). The Bible account read: Judges 10:15, 16; 11:1-40. Below are prepared answers to every question in the chapter — the discussion question, Dig Deeper, Reflect on the Lessons and Meditate on the Bigger Picture.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: In what ways did Jephthah and his daughter show courage?
cbs.answer: Jephthah showed courage by agreeing to lead God’s people after his half brothers had rejected and mistreated him — no bitterness. He tried peace first, and when war came he trusted Jehovah and made a sacred vow, knowing it might cost him what he loved most. His daughter showed even greater courage: she accepted the outcome willingly — “If you have opened your mouth to Jehovah, do to me as you have promised” — giving up marriage and motherhood to serve at the tabernacle. And Jephthah is named by Paul among the men of great faith in Hebrews 11:32.

scriptures.quote: But she said to him: “My father, if you have opened your mouth to Jehovah, do to me as you have promised, since Jehovah has executed vengeance for you upon your enemies, the Amʹmon·ites.”
And what more will I say? For time will fail me if I go on to relate about Gidʹe·on, Baʹrak, Samson, Jephʹthah, David, as well as Samuel and the other prophets.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 1
cbs.q: What indicates that the Ammonites were warring against not only the Israelites but also true worship? (it “Jephthah” ¶6)
cbs.answer: The answer is right in the reading. The Israelites had just repented: “They removed the foreign gods from their midst and served Jehovah.” (Judg 10:16) Only then did the Ammonites gather in Gilead for war. An attack on a freshly repentant nation serving the true God was an attack on true worship itself. That is why Jehovah took the war personally and gave Jephthah, by his spirit, such a decisive victory — and why the account teaches us that Jehovah defends those who return to him.

scriptures.quote: And they removed the foreign gods from their midst and served Jehovah, so that he could no longer tolerate Israel’s suffering.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 2
cbs.q: How was Jephthah’s attitude similar to that of Jacob when he made a vow to Jehovah? (it “Jephthah” ¶11)
cbs.answer: Both men made their vow in genuine faith and both treated it as absolutely binding. Jacob vowed at Bethel that if Jehovah brought him home safely, “Jehovah will certainly have proved to be my God” — and he returned to pay what he had promised. Jephthah likewise vowed to give to Jehovah whatever came out to meet him if victory was granted, and he carried it out despite the heartbreaking cost. For neither man was a vow a bargaining chip; it was sacred, made in faith and paid without delay.

scriptures.quote: and I return in peace to the house of my father, then Jehovah will certainly have proved to be my God.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 3
cbs.q: Why was it a real sacrifice for Jephthah to fulfill his vow? (w17.04 4 ¶6)
cbs.answer: Because the one who came out was his only child. Jephthah’s daughter was his only child; there was no son to carry on his name, so her devoted service at the tabernacle meant his family line in Israel would end. For a father in Israel that was a heavy loss — on top of the personal grief of giving up the daughter he loved. He paid the vow anyway. His courage was not only in the battle; it was in keeping his word to Jehovah at great personal cost.

scriptures.quote: Finally Jephʹthah came to his home in Mizʹpah, and look! his daughter was coming out to meet him, playing the tambourine and dancing! Now she was his one and only child. Besides her, he had neither son nor daughter.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 4
cbs.q: The prophet Samuel was born about the year 1180 B.C.E. What suggests that he and Jephthah’s daughter may have served at the tabernacle at the same time? (it “Jephthah” ¶2; see the timeline “From the Days of the Patriarchs to the Time of the Judges.”)
cbs.answer: After her father’s victory, Jephthah’s daughter went to serve at the tabernacle in Shiloh. Samuel, born about 1180 B.C.E., spent his boyhood serving at that same tabernacle under Eli. If her service fell in the late 1100s B.C.E., the period of Jephthah’s judgeship shown on the timeline, she would have been at Shiloh while Samuel was still a boy there. What a privilege it may have been for the selfless young woman to be near the future prophet of Israel!

cbs.label: Reflect · A
cbs.q: When parents show courage like Jephthah, what effect does it have on their children?
cbs.answer: Children watch what their parents do when obeying Jehovah costs something. A father who keeps his word to God even when it hurts, and a mother who stands for what is right in a hostile workplace, teach their children that Jehovah is worth any price. Jephthah’s daughter did not resist her father’s vow — she had evidently grown up valuing Jehovah above everything. Courage in parents builds courage in children; compromise in parents teaches children that faith is negotiable.

cbs.label: Reflect · B
cbs.q: How can Christians today imitate the young women who commended Jephthah’s daughter and helped her remain courageous?
cbs.answer: Those young women did not merely feel sorry for her — they spent four days a year with her, commending her selfless choice and comforting her grief. We can do the same: notice brothers and sisters who have accepted a hard assignment or suffered a real loss in Jehovah’s service, spend time with them, speak words of specific commendation, and stay in their lives — a visit, a call, an invitation to a meal. Regular encouragement keeps courageous people courageous.

cbs.label: Reflect · C
cbs.q: How might you imitate the courage of Jephthah and his daughter in your life?
cbs.answer: By paying what I promise Jehovah — serving him faithfully even when life changes direction. By putting sacred service ahead of personal plans, as Jephthah’s daughter did when she gave up marriage and motherhood. By refusing bitterness when others mistreat me, as Jephthah did with his half brothers. And by supporting the courageous decisions of my family members instead of standing in their way. Courage often shows itself not in one dramatic moment but in quietly keeping our dedication to Jehovah every day.

cbs.label: Meditate · A
cbs.q: What does this account teach me about Jehovah?
cbs.answer: That Jehovah detests what is detestable and values what is precious. He forbids human sacrifice — “whoever does these things is detestable to Jehovah” — so Jephthah’s vow was about whole-souled devotion, not death, and Jehovah accepted that devoted service. He is moved by faith: he gave Jephthah his spirit for the battle and rewarded a young woman’s willing sacrifice with a place in the inspired record. Jehovah never forgets those who give up much for him.

scriptures.quote: For whoever does these things is detestable to Jehovah, and on account of these detestable practices Jehovah your God is driving them away from before you.

cbs.label: Meditate · B
cbs.q: How does the account tie in with Jehovah’s purposes?
cbs.answer: Jehovah used Jephthah, empowered by his spirit, to deliver his people from the Ammonites, protecting true worship in Israel — the nation through which the promised Seed would come. The account is preserved among the great examples of faith: Paul includes Jephthah in Hebrews 11, where faithful ones of old — including the women who suffered great losses — look forward to attaining “a better resurrection” under God’s Kingdom. Jephthah’s story is part of the bigger story that ends in the restoration of all things.

scriptures.quote: Women received their dead by resurrection, but other men were tortured because they would not accept release by some ransom, in order that they might attain a better resurrection.

cbs.label: Meditate · C
cbs.q: What would I like to ask Jephthah and his daughter in the resurrection?
cbs.answer: To Jephthah: “What went through your mind as you walked home from that victory, wondering who would come out to meet you?” To his daughter: “Was there a moment you wished you could take back your words — and how did you find the strength to say ‘do to me as you have promised’? Did you ever meet the boy Samuel at the tabernacle?” I believe she would tell us what her whole account teaches: nothing given to Jehovah is ever lost.

wt.article: Guard Against “the Spirit of the World”

items.q: How does Satan use the spirit of the world? (1 John 2:15, 16)
items.comment: Satan uses the spirit of the world as his way of reaching us. He cannot be everywhere at once, and the Bible never says that any angel, good or bad, has that ability. But he has many wicked angels helping him, and the spirit they promote is everywhere. Most people breathe it in without realizing it. (1 John 2:15, 16) Even people who do not believe Satan exists do his will when they live by the world’s thinking — in a sense, they are “caught alive by him.”

scriptures.quote: Do not love either the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything in the world—the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the showy display of one’s means of life —does not originate with the Father, but originates with the world.
scriptures.use: Describes the world’s atmosphere that Satan promotes — the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes and the showy display of one’s means of life, none of which originates with the Father.

items.insight: Satan’s weapon is not a demon at every elbow — it is an atmosphere. The spirit of the world works like air: invisible, everywhere, and dangerous only when you stop noticing you are breathing it.
items.apply: This week, pick one habit — a show, a feed, a way of speaking — and ask honestly: ‘Whose spirit is this cultivating in me?’ Then change one thing about it.

paraNotes.points: Satan is not omnipresent — no angel has that ability — but he has many wicked angels, and the spirit of the world they promote is everywhere. Most people yield to it without realizing it (1 John 2:15, 16); even those who do not believe Satan exists please him when they act on it, being ‘caught alive by him’ (2 Tim 2:26).
paraNotes.highlight: Notice the precision: the article does not say Satan is everywhere — the Bible does not teach that. It is his influence, not his person, that surrounds us.

items.q: (a) How do Jehovah’s people differ from those who yield to “the spirit of the world”? (b) Of what danger do we need to be aware?
items.comment: Many of us once followed the spirit of the world ourselves. But when we learned who is behind it, we obeyed the Bible’s call to “reject ungodliness and worldly desires.” (Titus 2:11, 12) That is remarkable, considering Satan’s power — it shows we truly want Jehovah’s backing. Still, there is a danger to watch. The world appeals to our sinful tendencies in subtle ways, and some who fought hard for the faith later became infected by the world’s spirit. This study will show us how to avoid that outcome.

scriptures.quote: For the undeserved kindness of God has been manifested, bringing salvation to all sorts of people. It trains us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live with soundness of mind and righteousness and godly devotion amid this present system of things,
scriptures.use: Shows that God’s undeserved kindness trains us to reject ungodliness and worldly desires — the very opposite of the spirit of the world.

items.insight: Leaving the world’s spirit is not a one-time rescue; some who fought hard for the faith later became infected. The danger is not weakness at the start but drift over the years.
items.apply: Name one way the world’s thinking has changed since you came into the truth, and decide how you will push back against that drift this week.

paraNotes.points: Many of us once acted in accord with the world’s spirit, but on learning the truth we rejected it (Titus 2:11, 12). Doing so despite Satan’s widespread influence and enormous power shows we want Jehovah’s backing (Jas 4:7, 8).

The danger: the world appeals to our sinful tendencies subtly, and some who initially put up a hard fight for the faith later became infected (Eph 6:11; Phil 3:18). The article first defines ‘the spirit of the world’ (1 Cor 2:12).
paraNotes.highlight: Subtlety is the theme — the world rarely attacks front-on; it appeals to what is already inside us.

items.q: What is “the spirit of the world,” and how is it manifest today?
items.comment: In the Bible, “the spirit of the world” describes the way people who are not friends of God think and act. Those infected with it tend to be selfish, and they reject Jehovah’s moral standards. Many today take a permissive view of ungodly conduct — they follow “the will of the nations” rather than the will of the Creator. (1 Pet 4:3) It is a spirit, not merely a list of bad practices; it shapes how a whole world of people thinks, and that is why it can reach into our own thinking too.

scriptures.quote: For the time that has passed by is sufficient for you to have done the will of the nations when you carried on in acts of brazen conduct, unbridled passions, overdrinking, wild parties, drinking bouts, and lawless idolatries.
scriptures.use: Describes ‘the will of the nations’ — the permissive way of life that the spirit of the world promotes.

scriptures.quote: Now we received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit that is from God, so that we might know the things that have been kindly given us by God.
scriptures.use: Contrasts ‘the spirit of the world’ with the spirit that is from God, identifying the two opposing influences on our thinking.

items.insight: The spirit of the world is a way of THINKING, not just a list of deeds; that is why rejecting it starts in the mind, where the world reshapes what feels normal.
items.apply: When you notice a worldly idea presented as ‘enlightened,’ consciously state to yourself the Bible’s opposite view.

paraNotes.points: ‘The spirit of the world’ is the way people who are not friends of God think and act — selfish, rejecting Jehovah’s moral standards, permissive about ungodly conduct, following ‘the will of the nations’ (1 Pet 4:3).
paraNotes.highlight: The definition concerns thinking and acting — a spirit, not merely a style or a set of customs.

items.q: In what way is the world’s spirit like “the air”? (Ephesians 2:1, 2) (See also picture.)
items.comment: Paul compares the world’s spirit to “the air.” (Eph 2:1, 2) What a fitting illustration! Air is everywhere — you cannot escape it by staying home. And like polluted air, the spirit of the world is harmful yet easy to breathe in; a person can take it in without noticing, until it has affected him. It is one of Satan’s most effective means of “misleading the entire inhabited earth.” (Rev 12:9) Let us consider three subtle ways it can affect us.

scriptures.quote: Furthermore, God made you alive, though you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you at one time walked according to the system of things of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.
scriptures.use: Paul’s ‘air’ illustration: the world’s spirit surrounds people like the atmosphere — the ruler of the authority of the air works in the sons of disobedience.

scriptures.quote: So down the great dragon was hurled, the original serpent, the one called Devil and Satan, who is misleading the entire inhabited earth; he was hurled down to the earth, and his angels were hurled down with him.
scriptures.use: Identifies Satan as the one misleading the entire inhabited earth, using means such as the world’s spirit.

items.insight: Air is the perfect metaphor because the danger is not the poison we flee but the atmosphere we share. We live INSIDE the world’s spirit, so guarding has to be continuous — like breathing.
items.apply: Choose one ‘pollution source’ — a feed, a show, a kind of conversation — and reduce your exposure to it this week.

paraNotes.points: The world’s spirit is one of Satan’s effective means of misleading the entire inhabited earth (Rev 12:9). Paul likens it to ‘the air’ (Eph 2:1, 2): harmful, everywhere, and easy to breathe in. Three subtle influences will now be considered.
paraNotes.highlight: Look at the picture with this paragraph — ‘The spirit of the world is easy to breathe in’ — exactly the point of the ‘air’ illustration.

items.q: How is the spirit of the world evident in people’s speech?
items.comment: The Bible foretold that in the last days people would be “boastful, haughty,” and “not open to any agreement.” (2 Tim 3:2, 3) We see those traits in speech all around us: news reports tell of verbal disputes that escalate into violence, abusive speech is common in many homes, and obscene language comes from the mouths of adults and children alike. (Eph 5:3, 4) Such speech is not just bad manners — it is evidence that the spirit of the world is at work in people’s hearts.

scriptures.quote: For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, haughty, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, disloyal, having no natural affection, not open to any agreement, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, without love of goodness,
scriptures.use: Foretells the last-days traits that now show up in people’s speech: boastful, haughty, not open to any agreement.

items.insight: Speech is the world’s spirit made audible — the last-days traits Paul listed show up first in how people talk, and they are now treated as normal.
items.apply: For one day, monitor your tone and word choice in your closest relationships — that is where harshness hides first.

paraNotes.points: Last-days people display boastfulness, haughtiness and being ‘not open to any agreement’ in their speech (2 Tim 3:1-3): verbal disputes escalate into violence, abusive speech is common in homes, and obscene language is heard from adults and children alike (Eph 5:3, 4).
paraNotes.highlight: Notice how ordinary the examples are — this is speech you can overhear at a bus stop, which is exactly why it is easy to breathe in.

items.q: How can we examine our speech?
items.comment: Whether we speak in person or by text, our speech should be exemplary. (Jas 1:26) So we do well to examine ourselves: Do I use foul language when I am provoked — perhaps with people who do not know that I serve Jehovah? Have my conversations with fellow believers become negative, cynical, sarcastic? Do I speak harshly to my family members? What would they honestly say about my speech? Their answer may reveal something our own ears have stopped noticing.

scriptures.quote: If any man thinks he is a worshipper of God but does not keep a tight rein on his tongue, he is deceiving his own heart, and his worship is futile.
scriptures.use: Links the tongue to worship: one who does not control his tongue deceives his own heart and his worship is futile.

items.insight: Jehovah connects speech to worship — foul talk is not merely rude, it nullifies worship. The tongue is the first place to examine, and the people who know us best are the honest witnesses.
items.apply: Decide now what you will say — and what you will not say — the next time you are provoked.

paraNotes.points: Our speech should be exemplary in person and electronically (Jas 1:26, 27). Test questions: Do I use foul language when provoked, perhaps with people who don’t know I am one of Jehovah’s Witnesses? Have talks with fellow believers turned negative, cynical, sarcastic? Do I speak harshly to my family — and what would they say about my speech?
paraNotes.highlight: Notice the two audiences that matter most: strangers who may learn from our speech who we are, and our own family, who hear it every day.

items.q: How can we shun unwholesome speech? (Colossians 3:8-10)
items.comment: If our speech reflects the world’s spirit, we must change more than our words. Jesus said: “Whatever comes out of the mouth comes from the heart.” (Matt 15:18) Speech usually reflects how we feel inside, which is why the Bible links abusive speech with anger, wrath and malicious bitterness. (Eph 4:31) So we ask Jehovah to help us cultivate “the new personality,” we research our publications for help, and we are resolved not to let the world’s spirit pollute our speech. (Col 3:8-10; Eph 4:29)

scriptures.quote: However, whatever comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and those things defile a man.
scriptures.use: Jesus shows that speech flows from the heart, so lasting change in speech requires a change of heart.

scriptures.quote: Put away from yourselves every kind of malicious bitterness, anger, wrath, screaming, and abusive speech, as well as everything injurious.
scriptures.use: Links abusive speech with the negative emotions that produce it.

scriptures.quote: But now you must put them all away from you: wrath, anger, badness, abusive speech, and obscene talk out of your mouth. Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old personality with its practices, and clothe yourselves with the new personality, which through accurate knowledge is being made new according to the image of the One who created it,
scriptures.use: The practical prescription: put away wrath, anger, abusive speech and obscene talk, strip off the old personality and clothe yourselves with the new personality.

scriptures.quote: Let a rotten word not come out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up as the need may be, to impart what is beneficial to the hearers.
scriptures.use: The positive goal: words that build up and impart benefit to the hearers.

items.insight: You cannot fix speech by vocabulary alone — the heart produces the words. Cultivating ‘the new personality’ on the inside is what cleans up the speech on the outside.
items.apply: Research one article in our publications on wholesome speech this week, and share one point from it with your family.

paraNotes.points: Change more than words: speech reflects the heart (Matt 15:18), and abusive speech is linked with anger, wrath and malicious bitterness (Eph 4:31). Pray for help to cultivate ‘the new personality’ (Col 3:8-10), research the publications, and resolve not to let the world’s spirit pollute your speech (Eph 4:29).

items.q: How is the world’s spirit evident in the way people view Jehovah’s moral standards?
items.comment: Today the world openly condones — even encourages — abortion, homosexuality, and premarital sex. (Isa 5:20) If we are not careful, that spirit can gradually weaken our hatred for what is bad. (2 Cor 11:3) We might even begin to think the world’s view is enlightened and Jehovah’s standards are outdated. Nothing could be further from the truth. Jehovah’s ways are always for our good; they are higher than man’s ways and they never go out of date. (Isa 55:9)

scriptures.quote: Woe to those who say that good is bad and bad is good, Those who substitute darkness for light and light for darkness, Those who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!
scriptures.use: Foretells the world’s inverted moral compass — calling good bad and bad good, exactly the permissive view of Jehovah’s standards today.

scriptures.quote: “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, So my ways are higher than your ways And my thoughts than your thoughts.
scriptures.use: Answers the claim that God’s standards are outdated: his ways and thoughts are higher than man’s and never become outdated.

items.insight: Isaiah’s ‘woe’ shows how inverted the world’s moral compass is — the world does not merely break God’s standards; it congratulates itself for doing so.
items.apply: Check your entertainment queue this week: does anything on it celebrate what Jehovah hates?

paraNotes.points: The world condones or even encourages abortion, homosexuality and premarital sex (Isa 5:20); its spirit can gradually weaken our hatred for what is bad (2 Cor 11:3). Jehovah’s ways are always for our good — higher than man’s ways and never outdated (Isa 48:17, 18; 55:9).

items.q: How can we examine our view of the things that Jehovah hates?
items.comment: Those who want to please Jehovah must hate what he hates. (Ps 97:10) So we examine ourselves with honest questions: Do I feel that Jehovah’s moral laws are keeping me from living as I would really like? Does my choice of entertainment show that I am drawn to things that Jehovah hates? Do I wish that Jehovah would somehow adjust his standards to conform to my desires? How we answer those questions reveals whose spirit is really shaping us.

scriptures.quote: you who love Jehovah, hate what is bad. He is guarding the lives of his loyal ones; He rescues them from the hand of the wicked.
scriptures.use: Jehovah’s servants are to hate what is bad — the standard against which our view of his moral laws must be measured.

items.insight: ‘Hate what is bad’ is a feeling Jehovah expects us to cultivate — and the test questions (entertainment, wishing his standards would bend) target exactly where our affections sit.
items.apply: Pray for Jehovah’s help to hate what he hates — and name to yourself one specific thing you have been tolerating for too long.

paraNotes.points: Pleasing Jehovah means hating what he hates (Ps 97:10). The test questions: Do I feel his moral laws keep me from living as I would like? Does my entertainment show I am drawn to what he hates? Do I wish his standards would adjust to my desires?

items.q: How can we learn to hate the things that Jehovah hates?
items.comment: If you feel drawn to something that Jehovah hates, do not conclude that it is impossible for you to live by his standards. All imperfect humans are inclined to sin. (Ps 51:5; 103:14) But you can choose not to act on wrong desires and refuse to dwell on them. When a wrong desire comes up, immediately turn your eyes and your mind away, and reflect on how giving in would damage your relationship with Jehovah and with others. (Gen 39:9, 12) With his help, you can learn to hate what is bad.

scriptures.quote: There is no one greater in this house than I am, and he has not withheld from me anything at all except you, because you are his wife. So how could I commit this great badness and actually sin against God?” ... Then she grabbed hold of him by his garment and said: “Lie down with me!” But he left his garment in her hand and fled outside.
scriptures.use: Joseph’s response: he refused to dwell on the desire and then physically ran from it — immediate, decisive action, not negotiation.

items.insight: Feeling drawn to what Jehovah hates is not failure — it is the common experience of imperfect humans. The sin begins when we feed the desire instead of turning away instantly.
items.apply: Rehearse your ‘turn away’ move in advance — decide exactly what you will physically do the moment a wrong desire surfaces.

paraNotes.points: Being drawn to what Jehovah hates does not make obedience impossible — all imperfect humans are inclined to sin (Ps 51:5; 103:14). Choose not to act on wrong desires, refuse to dwell on them, turn eyes and mind away immediately (Gen 39:9, 12), and reflect on the damage giving in would do (Eph 5:5).
paraNotes.highlight: Joseph’s response was physical and immediate — he ran. The counsel is to move, not to negotiate with the desire.

items.q: How is the world’s spirit reflected on the Internet?
items.comment: The Internet touches nearly every part of our life, even our worship — yet much of what is found there promotes the spirit of the world. Pornography is widespread and easy to reach; sexting is rampant, especially among youths. There is propaganda that distorts reality, and social media posts show only the highlights of people’s lives, which can stir a craving for recreation and travel — even at the expense of our worship. (Heb 10:24, 25) We need to notice how these things tug at us.

scriptures.quote: And let us consider one another so as to incite to love and fine works, not forsaking our meeting together, as some have the custom, but encouraging one another, and all the more so as you see the day drawing near.
scriptures.use: The standard the online world can quietly erode: love and fine works, and meeting together — which highlight-reel living can make feel dull by comparison.

items.insight: The Internet is not a neutral space — much of it is engineered to promote the world’s spirit: pornography, distorted narratives, envy through highlight reels. Use it as a tool, not a dwelling.
items.apply: Set a specific time limit on recreational scrolling this week — and keep it.

paraNotes.points: Much of the Internet promotes the world’s spirit: widespread pornography, rampant sexting especially among youths, propaganda that distorts reality, and social media highlight reels that can push worship aside (Heb 10:24, 25).
paraNotes.highlight: Notice that the trap is not only immorality — envy and time-loss through ‘the highlights of people’s lives’ are also the world’s spirit at work.

items.q: How can we evaluate our use of the Internet?
items.comment: We can evaluate our use of the Internet with honest questions: How much time do I spend scrolling with no specific reason? (Eph 5:15, 16) What kind of content do I allow myself to be exposed to, and how quickly do I turn away from what is objectionable? (Ps 119:37) Am I quick to believe everything I read online, or do I check the facts? (Prov 14:15) Our answers show whether the Internet is serving us — or the world’s spirit is using it to serve itself.

scriptures.quote: So keep strict watch that how you walk is not as unwise but as wise persons, making the best use of your time, because the days are wicked.
scriptures.use: Paul’s counsel to keep strict watch over how we walk and make the best use of our time applies directly to aimless scrolling.

scriptures.quote: Turn my eyes away from looking at what is worthless; Preserve me alive in your way.
scriptures.use: The prayer for anyone online: turn my eyes away from looking at what is worthless.

scriptures.quote: The naive person believes every word, But the shrewd one ponders each step.
scriptures.use: The antidote to online propaganda: the shrewd one ponders each step instead of believing every word.

items.insight: Aimless scrolling is the subtle danger — it is how the air gets in. The test is not ‘Is it wrong?’ but ‘Is it wise? Is it feeding faith or starving it?’
items.apply: Before opening a feed this week, ask: ‘Why am I here, and what will I gain?’ If there is no answer, close the app.

paraNotes.points: Evaluate with questions: How much time do I spend scrolling without a specific reason? (Eph 5:15, 16) What content do I allow, and how quickly do I turn away from what is objectionable? (Ps 119:37) Am I quick to believe everything online, or do I check the facts? (Prov 14:15)

items.q: How can we avoid online dangers?
items.comment: To guard against the spirit of the world, limit the time you spend online and avoid looking at anything inappropriate. Parents should also carefully monitor their children’s use of social media. (Eph 6:4) That counsel is practical, not extreme: many researchers have found that youths who spend much time on social media are more likely to be lonely, anxious and depressed. When we apply the practical counsel found in God’s Word, we can avoid the online dangers that the world’s spirit uses to reach us.

scriptures.quote: And fathers, do not be irritating your children, but go on bringing them up in the discipline and admonition of Jehovah.
scriptures.use: Parents’ responsibility: bring children up in the discipline and admonition of Jehovah — which includes monitoring what they view online.

items.insight: Researchers confirm what the Bible implies: heavy social media use harms youths emotionally. Jehovah’s counsel is protective, not restrictive.
items.apply: Parents: review your children’s social media use with them this week — calmly and together, not as a police raid.

paraNotes.points: Limit online time, avoid anything inappropriate, and parents should carefully monitor children’s social media (Eph 6:4). Research finds heavy social-media youths are more likely to be lonely, anxious and depressed.
paraNotes.highlight: Practical, not extreme: the Bible’s counsel matches what researchers find — applying God’s Word protects us from online dangers.

items.q: What do you learn from Gloria’s experience? (See also picture.)
items.comment: Gloria learned the truth at an early age, but the desire for fame and money pulled at her. She neglected the meetings and soon did not want to be a Witness anymore. When she recognized that her goals were shaped by the world’s spirit, she acted: she increased her time in personal Bible study and prayer, and she cut off association with people who were not serving Jehovah. Now she is rich with spiritual blessings. If we find the world’s spirit has affected us, we can take the same steps.
items.insight: Gloria’s recovery was not passive — she increased study and prayer AND changed her association. Correcting course requires both feeding the spirit and starving the world’s influence.
items.apply: If you sense drift, schedule one concrete correction this week: an extra study session, a change in prayer, or a change of association.

paraNotes.points: Gloria, drawn by a desire for fame and money, neglected the meetings; when she recognized the world’s spirit in her goals, she increased Bible study and prayer and cut off association with those not serving Jehovah — now she is ‘rich with spiritual blessings.’
paraNotes.highlight: See the picture ‘What can you do to resist the spirit of the world?’ Footnote a: the names in this article have been changed.

items.q: What does Robert’s experience teach you?
items.comment: Robert’s schoolmates and unwholesome entertainment shaped his life — smoking, drinking, homosexuality. He felt he had freedom to do as he wanted, but in time he saw the truth: he was not free at all; he had become a slave to the world. (2 Pet 2:19) So he made changes — he surrounded himself with people who love Jehovah and changed how he carried himself, how he dressed and groomed, and even how he spoke. Now he wakes up every day aware of his clean life, and it makes him feel truly rich.

scriptures.quote: While they are promising them freedom, they themselves are slaves of corruption; for if anyone is overcome by someone, he is his slave.
scriptures.use: Exposes the world’s lie: what promises freedom actually enslaves — exactly what Robert discovered.

items.insight: Robert’s story proves that ‘freedom’ as the world defines it is a lie — doing as he wanted made him a slave. Real freedom came through changed association and changed conduct.
items.apply: Choose your association deliberately this week: one contact that strengthens you, one that weakens you — and be honest about which is which.

paraNotes.points: Robert’s ‘freedom’ was slavery to the world (2 Pet 2:19). He surrounded himself with people who love Jehovah and changed his conduct, dress, grooming and speech — a clean life now makes him feel truly rich.

items.q: Why can you be certain that you can resist the spirit of this world? (1 John 4:4)
items.comment: We can be certain we can resist, because Jehovah is far more powerful than Satan and his wicked world. (1 John 4:4) What is more, Jehovah stands ready to give us his holy spirit — the most powerful force in the universe — to help us avoid the world’s influence. (Luke 11:13) So the course is clear: keep “walking by [God’s] spirit,” shunning unwholesome speech, rejecting immoral conduct and avoiding online dangers, and we will guard against the spirit of the world. (Gal 5:16)

scriptures.quote: You originate with God, little children, and you have conquered them, because the one who is in union with you is greater than the one who is in union with the world.
scriptures.use: The ground of our confidence: the one in union with us is greater than the one in union with the world.

scriptures.quote: Therefore, if you, although being wicked, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more so will the Father in heaven give holy spirit to those asking him!”
scriptures.use: The specific help Jesus promised: the Father in heaven gives holy spirit to those asking him.

scriptures.quote: But I say, Keep walking by spirit and you will carry out no fleshly desire at all.
scriptures.use: The daily course: keep walking by spirit and no fleshly desire — the world’s appeal — will carry us away.

items.insight: The article closes with simple arithmetic: Jehovah’s power minus Satan’s power equals our certainty. Victory is not in doubt; our part is to keep walking by God’s spirit.
items.apply: Ask for holy spirit by name in your prayers this week — it is the specific help Jesus said the Father gives to those asking him. (Luke 11:13)

paraNotes.points: Reject the spirit of this world: shun unwholesome speech, reject immoral conduct, avoid online dangers. Jehovah is far more powerful than Satan and his world (1 John 4:4), and he gives his holy spirit — the most powerful force in the universe — to help (Luke 11:13); keep walking by God’s spirit (Gal 5:16).
paraNotes.highlight: The certainty rests not on our willpower but on Jehovah’s power and his spirit — the closing security of the whole article.

recap.q: How can we guard against “the spirit of the world” with respect to our speech?
recap.comment: We remember that whatever comes out of the mouth comes from the heart. We examine ourselves honestly — how we speak when provoked, how we talk to our family, whether our conversations with fellow believers have turned negative or cynical — and we ask Jehovah to help us cultivate the new personality and put away abusive speech, using words that build others up.

recap.q: How can we guard against “the spirit of the world” with respect to our view of immoral conduct?
recap.comment: We keep our hatred for what is bad strong, refusing to let the world’s permissive view weaken it. We do not act on wrong desires or dwell on them; when a wrong desire comes up, we immediately turn our eyes and mind away, trusting that Jehovah’s standards are always for our good, higher than man’s ways, and never outdated.

recap.q: How can we guard against “the spirit of the world” with respect to our use of the Internet?
recap.comment: We limit the time we spend online, avoid anything inappropriate, and monitor what our children view. We are careful about content that consumes time or distorts our thinking, and we check facts instead of believing everything we read. Applying the Bible’s practical counsel keeps us safe from the online dangers the world’s spirit uses.

daily.comment: Each of us has an important role to play in making the spiritual paradise attractive to others. We can fulfill this role if we imitate Jehovah. He does not drag people into his organization against their will. Instead, he gently “draws” people to himself. ( John 6:44; Jer. 31:3 ) Good-hearted people who learn about Jehovah’s loving qualities and appealing personality are irresistibly drawn to him. How can we, by our good qualities and fine conduct, attract people to the spiritual paradise? One way is by treating our fellow worshippers with love and kindness. When new ones attend our congregation meetings, we want them to come to the same conclusion as did the unbelievers who likely attended the meetings in ancient Corinth. They declared: “God is really among you.” ( 1 Cor. 14:24, 25; Zech. 8:23 ) Thus, we must continue to heed the counsel in today’s text. w24.04 23-24 ¶16-17 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: He opened up their minds fully to grasp the meaning of the Scriptures.​
daily.comment: Jesus’ disciples accepted God’s Word and tried hard to apply it in their life. ( John 17:6 ) Still, Jesus’ dying as a criminal on a torture stake confused them. Jesus realized that their doubts stemmed, not from a bad heart, but from a lack of understanding. ( Luke 9:44, 45; John 20:9 ) So he taught them to reason on the Scriptures. Consider how he did that when he appeared to the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Jesus did not immediately tell the men who he was. Instead, he asked questions. Why? Perhaps he wanted them to express what was on their mind and in their heart. And they did. They told him that they had expected Jesus to deliver Israel from Roman oppression. ( Luke 24:18-27 ) Jesus used the Scriptures to help the men to understand what had happened. Later that evening, Jesus spent time assuring the other disciples of these truths.​— Luke 24:33-48 . w24.10 14 ¶9-10 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: I do nothing of my own initiative; but just as the Father taught me, I speak these things.​
daily.comment: Jesus learned from his heavenly Father what to do and what to say. Following the example of Jesus, Jehovah’s organization bases its moral teachings and its direction on God’s Word. ( 2 Tim. 3:16, 17 ) We regularly receive reminders to read and apply God’s Word. We benefit greatly when we study the Bible with the help of our Christian publications. For instance, we are able to compare Bible teachings with the direction we receive from the organization. When we see that the guidance we receive is based on the Scriptures, our confidence in Jehovah’s organization grows. ( Rom. 12:2 ) Jesus preached “the good news of the Kingdom of God.” ( Luke 4:43, 44 ) Also, Jesus commanded his disciples to preach about the Kingdom. ( Luke 9:1, 2; 10:8, 9 ) Today all who are associated with Jehovah’s organization preach the Kingdom message no matter where they live. w24.04 9 ¶5-7 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: We will do all that you have commanded, and we will go wherever you send us.​
daily.comment: Maintain confidence in theocratic direction. In ancient Israel, Jehovah used Moses and then Joshua to convey instructions to His people. ( Josh. 1:17 ) The Israelites were blessed when they viewed these men as representatives of Jehovah God. Centuries later when the Christian congregation was first formed, the 12 apostles gave direction. ( Acts 8:14, 15 ) Then that group was expanded to include other elders in Jerusalem. By following the guidance received from those faithful men, “the congregations continued to be made firm in the faith and to increase in number day by day.” ( Acts 16:4, 5 ) In modern times, we too are blessed when we follow theocratic direction from Jehovah’s organization. w24.07 10 ¶10 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: I have found David the son of Jesse a man agreeable to my heart.​
daily.comment: Jehovah dearly loved King David. He even called him “a man agreeable to my heart.” But David became involved in gross sins, including adultery and murder. According to the Mosaic Law, David deserved to die. ( Lev. 20:10; Num. 35:31 ) Yet, Jehovah kindly stepped in. He sent his prophet Nathan to visit the king, even though David had not yet shown any sign of repentance. Nathan used an illustration designed to touch David’s heart. Deeply moved, David repented. ( 2 Sam. 12:1-14 ) He wrote a heartfelt psalm that reveals his repentant spirit. ( Ps. 51 , superscription) That psalm has comforted countless sinners and motivated them to repent. Are we not glad that Jehovah lovingly led his beloved servant David to repentance? w24.08 10 ¶9 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: Prove to yourselves the good and acceptable and perfect will of God.​
daily.comment: Many would agree that being a parent is a full-time job. If you are a parent with a young child, we commend you for working hard to build strong faith in him. ( Deut. 6:6, 7 ) As your child grows up, he may begin asking serious questions about our Bible-based beliefs, including the Bible’s moral standards. At first, you may be worried about your child’s questions. You might even view such questions as a step backward regarding his faith. In reality, however, growing children need to ask questions in order to form their own convictions. ( 1 Cor. 13:11 ) So there is no reason to be fearful. You may view all sincere questions your child raises about our beliefs as opportunities to help him to develop his thinking ability. w24.12 14 ¶1-2 November 30–December 6

daily.scripture: We are . . . the sort who have faith for the preserving of our lives.​
daily.comment: The Hebrew Christians would need strong faith to survive the approaching tribulation in Judea. ( Heb. 10:37, 38 ) Jesus had warned his followers that when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by encamped armies, they should flee to the mountains. His counsel applied to all Christians, whether they lived in that city or in the open countryside. ( Luke 21:20-24 ) People back then who were threatened by an invading army would normally seek protection in a walled city like Jerusalem. Fleeing to the mountains would have seemed illogical and would have taken great faith. The Hebrew Christians would also need to trust those whom Jesus was using to direct the congregation. Those taking the lead likely gave specific instructions to help all in the congregation to follow Jesus’ direction at the right time and in an orderly manner.​— Heb. 13:17 . w24.09 10 ¶9-10 November 30–December 6
